The peruke, or periwig, was a full-bottomed wig made of human or animal hair and often dusted with white or colored powder, becoming the dominant masculine fashion accessory from the sixteen sixties through the eighteen hundreds. Originating in France under Louis XIV, the peruke symbolized wealth, status, and gentility, transforming every well-dressed man into a walking advertisement of his social position and fashion sensibility.

Originally adopted to cover baldness and male pattern hair loss, the peruke quickly became fashionable among men with full hair, with wearing one signaling membership in the upper classes. The full-bottomed peruke featured long curls cascading down the back and shoulders, requiring significant amounts of expensive human hair and skilled tailors and wigmakers to achieve the style. Perukes were powdered with white, gray, or even tinted powders—wheat flour mixed with scent and color—making the powder expensive and marking the wearer as wealthy enough to discard it daily.

Maintenance was elaborate. Perukes were dressed on wooden blocks, curled with irons, powdered, and stored carefully, with a gentleman often owning several for different occasions. The peruke symbolized the age of absolute monarchy and aristocratic refinement. French court fashion made the peruke an international status symbol across Europe. It gradually simplified from massive full-bottomed versions to smaller, neater styles as the eighteenth century progressed. By eighteen hundred, wigs had become less fashionable for younger men.

Powdered wigs persisted longest in formal dress, legal professions, and military uniforms, where they survive in limited use into the present day. British judges and barristers still wear them. The peruke's dominance reflects the fashion authority of Louis XIV, the French king whose court established the peruke as the essential mark of gentlemanly status. It remained significant through the reign of George III, the English king during the peak of peruke fashion in Britain. The garment's gradual decline was part of the Enlightenment, the era associated with rational dress reform that began questioning the peruke's necessity.
